hook_text: Summer is when the Earth is closest to the sun, right? Wrong. We are closest in January, and Europe is freezing.
clip_script: Here is the truth about summer. The Earth goes round the sun once a year, and it is closest in early January. But January is deep winter in Europe. So distance cannot be the reason. The real reason is the lean. The Earth's axis is tilted about twenty-three and a half degrees, and it keeps pointing the same way all year, like a leaning top going round a lamp. In December our half of the world leans towards the sun. At midday the sun stands overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, in Limpopo, and in Johannesburg it climbs to about eighty-seven and a half degrees. Tiny shadows, strong heat. In June we lean away. The sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, way up in the Sahara, and Johannesburg's midday sun drops to forty and a half degrees. Long shadows, weak heat. Straight torch, hot spot. Tilted torch, weak glow. It is the lean, not the distance.
visual_style: A whiteboard orbit with a tilted Earth at four positions, an arrow showing the axis always pointing the same way, a stick in a school yard casting a tiny December shadow and a long June shadow.
pacing: Sharp hook, quick debunk, then the tilt and the two shadows side by side.
